(CNN) -- For actress Kyra Sedgwick, it's the public's approval that makes it worth being away from her family for six months to tape her critically acclaimed series "The Closer." Kyra Sedgwick and her husband, Kevin Bacon, at the 66th annual Golden Globe Awards this month. But she may be getting more approval from her peers, too. Sedgwick will walk the red carpet again Sunday night at the Screen Actors Guild Awards, where she is nominated for a fourth consecutive year for outstanding performance by a female actor in a drama series for her role as Deputy Chief Brenda Johnson. She's also won a Golden Globe for her performance, in 2007. The TNT series resumes Monday night where it left off in September with what Sedgwick called "a fantastic five episodes." (TNT is a unit of Time Warner, as is CNN.) "I said to the writers, 'I really want a lot of personal stuff for Brenda,' " Sedgwick said. "I feel like there's some of those personal quiet moments with her alone, is something that I've been missing as an actor, and I feel like the audience has been missing, too. "She is such a complicated, fascinating character, and watching her growth and lack of growth is something that is really interesting," she said. When CNN asked whether the new episodes might include a wedding for her character, Sedgwick laughed. "That might very well happen," she said. "That's pretty insightful of you. I'm just going to just say that." A marriage for Brenda Johnson would be "a complicated, difficult situation," she said, because "she's basically married to her work." Sedgwick's job also complicates her real-life marriage to Bacon, since the show is produced in Los Angeles and the couple lives in Connecticut with their two children. That's where the approval -- whether on the street from fans or at award shows -- has "been a wonderful phenomenon for me," she said. "On a personal level, that's really good for me, because I really miss my family when I'm working on the show six months in L.A.," she said. "As much as I try to get my kids to move to L.A. and my husband, they just wouldn't have it. "It's challenging, and I'm glad that people are watching, because otherwise it would be kind of hard to go to work," Sedgwick said. Sedgwick has moved into an executive producer's role on the show, which she said she expects to continue for at least two more years. "I love being with a group where there's not a power struggle," she said. "I have a lot of say, and I always have. And that feels really good." CNN Radio's Jackie Howard contributed to this report .

Sedgwick, who portrays the sharp-tongued Deputy Chief Brenda Leigh Johnson on the police procedural, recently earned a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for her performance, adding to a growing list of accolades for her work on the series.

"Brenda is such a wonderfully complicated character," Sedgwick said. "She's brilliant at her job but often a mess in her personal life. There's something really honest about that contradiction that I think audiences connect with."

"At the end of the day, I get to do what I love and go home to the people I love," she said. "Not everyone gets that, and I don't take it for granted."

# An Evening with Kyra Sedgwick: On "The Closer," Craft, and Keeping It Real

*In this exclusive sit-down, the Emmy-winning actress opens up about her signature role, the pressures of critical acclaim, and the marriage that keeps her grounded.*

---

Kyra Sedgwick settles into her chair with the easy warmth of someone who has learned to enjoy the ride. For years, audiences have known her as Deputy Chief Brenda Leigh Johnson—the deceptively sweet, deeply relentless investigator whose Southern charm masks a razor-sharp interrogator. Today, she's ready to talk about all of it.

**Q: Brenda Johnson has become one of television's most beloved characters. What is it about her that continues to captivate you?**

"What I love about Brenda is her contradictions," Sedgwick says, leaning forward. "She can be manipulative in the interview room, ruthless in pursuit of a confession, and then completely fall apart trying to manage her personal life. She's a mess and a genius at the same time. That's a gift for any actor. You never run out of things to explore."

**Q: She's famous for that final push in the interrogation room—the moment suspects crack. How do you approach those scenes?**

"They're exhausting, honestly," she laughs. "But they're my favorite. There's a rhythm to it, almost musical. Brenda listens more than people realize. That sweetness isn't a trick—part of her genuinely connects with people, even the ones she's about to put away. I try to find that human thread every time."

**Q: What can fans expect from the upcoming episodes?**

"Things get personal," she teases. "We're going to see Brenda's carefully constructed walls really tested—both at work and at home. There's a case coming up that hits close to who she is, and it forces her to confront the cost of doing this job the way she does it. The writers have been fearless this season. I think viewers are going to be surprised."

**Q: Your work has earned significant awards recognition, including major nominations and wins. How do you handle that kind of acclaim?**

Sedgwick pauses, choosing her words carefully. "It's humbling, and it's a little terrifying. Awards are lovely, but they can mess with your head if you let them. I try to remember that the recognition is really about the whole team—the writers, my castmates, the crew who show up before dawn. I just happen to be the face standing at the podium. When I won, I was genuinely shocked. I don't think that feeling ever fully goes away."

**Q: You've been married to Kevin Bacon for a long time in an industry not known for lasting marriages. What's the secret?**

Her whole demeanor softens. "We laugh a lot. That's the honest answer. We take each other seriously as artists but not too seriously as people. Kevin keeps me humble—he's not remotely impressed by any of the Hollywood stuff, and neither am I, really. We made a decision early on to put the family first, to be present for our kids, and to keep dating each other even after all these years."

**Q: Does having two working actors under one roof ever create competition?**

"You'd think so, but no," she says, shaking her head. "We root for each other. When one of us gets a great role, the other one is genuinely thrilled. We've been each other's first readers, first critics, first cheerleaders for decades. That partnership is the thing I'm proudest of—more than any trophy on a shelf."

**Q: Any chance we'll see the two of you working together again?**

"Oh, we love working together," she grins. "The trick is finding the right project. When it's right, you'll know. Until then, I'm perfectly happy stealing kisses between takes on our own separate sets."

---

As the interview wraps, Sedgwick offers a parting thought about longevity—in her career and her marriage. "You show up, you do the work, you stay curious, and you don't take any of it for granted. That's true for Brenda, and it's true for me."

Spoken like someone who, both on screen and off, knows exactly how to close.

**By CNN Entertainment Staff**

Television actress Elena Marchetti has secured her first Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Drama Series, recognition that comes after years of steady work in supporting roles before her recent breakthrough.

Marchetti, 34, earned the nod for her portrayal of Detective Sarah Whitmore in the critically acclaimed series "Harbor Lines," which follows a homicide investigator navigating both crime scenes and her own complicated past in a fictional coastal town.

"Elena brought layers to Sarah that weren't even on the page," Ashford said in a statement. "There's a scene in the sixth episode where she barely says a word for four minutes, and yet you understand everything her character is feeling. That's the mark of a truly gifted performer."

"The hardest part is missing bedtime stories when we're shooting late," she admitted. "But my husband is my anchor. He kept our world running while I disappeared into this character for months. This nomination belongs to him just as much as it does to me."

Marchetti added that she hopes her journey encourages other actors who have taken longer paths to recognition.

"I spent a lot of years wondering if my moment would ever come," she said. "So to anyone still waiting—keep going. It's never too late."
